track.name: sql-analytics
track.label: SQL for Business Analysts
track.summary: Master SQL from first queries to window functions and real-world business reporting — learn to query databases, combine tables, aggregate data, and write the analyses that drive data-driven decisions.

phases.title: SQL Foundations
phases.description: Write your first real queries — SELECT, WHERE, ORDER BY, GROUP BY, and HAVING — and understand why SQL beats spreadsheets for large datasets.

phases.title: Joins & Relationships
phases.description: Combine data across multiple tables using INNER, LEFT, RIGHT, and FULL JOINs, and learn to read entity-relationship diagrams so you know which tables to join.

phases.title: Aggregations & Window Functions
phases.description: Go beyond GROUP BY — partition aggregates, rank rows, and compute LEAD/LAG differences and running totals without collapsing your result set.

phases.title: CTEs & Subqueries
phases.description: Break complex queries into readable building blocks using WITH clauses, nested SELECTs, and query decomposition techniques that make code easier to review and maintain.

phases.title: Real Business Queries
phases.description: Apply SQL to the reports analysts actually produce — cohort analysis, funnel drop-off, churn, retention, and revenue breakdowns.

phases.title: BigQuery & Cloud SQL
phases.description: Move from local practice to the cloud — spin up BigQuery's free sandbox, explore public datasets, and learn to write cost-efficient queries.

topics.title: SELECT, WHERE, and ORDER BY
topics.description: Write your first queries — choose columns with SELECT, filter rows with WHERE, and sort results with ORDER BY.

steps.d: Query a table and name specific columns — SELECT customer_id, order_date, amount FROM orders — instead of SELECT *.
Add WHERE amount > 1000 to show only large orders, or WHERE order_date >= '2024-01-01' to show only recent transactions.
Use ORDER BY amount DESC to sort from highest to lowest, or ORDER BY order_date ASC to sort from oldest to newest.
Add LIMIT 10 to return only the first 10 rows, useful for exploring a large table without pulling millions of rows.
Check that you got the columns you asked for, the rows match your filter condition, and the sort order is correct by spot-checking a few values.

topics.title: GROUP BY, HAVING, and Aggregate Functions
topics.description: Summarise datasets with COUNT, SUM, and AVG, group them with GROUP BY, and filter groups with the HAVING clause.

steps.d: Collapse rows by region using GROUP BY region to see how many orders came from each region.
Apply COUNT, SUM, and AVG to grouped data — GROUP BY region SELECT region, COUNT(*), SUM(amount), AVG(amount).
Use HAVING SUM(amount) > 100000 to show only regions with total sales above $100k, filtering after aggregation.
Use GROUP BY region, product_category to see sales by region AND product, breaking out the data two ways at once.
Sum the aggregated values and verify they match the original total, confirming your GROUP BY logic is correct.

topics.title: Databases vs. Spreadsheets
topics.description: Understand when SQL beats Excel — relational structure, millions of rows, reproducibility, and the limits of each tool.

steps.d: Take a 10,000-row dataset, compute SUM and COUNT in Excel and in SQL, and compare the performance — SQL should be much faster.

Sketch a database structure for an e-commerce business with separate customers, orders, and products tables, showing how each table relates to the others, so you see why normalization enables faster queries.
Show how a SQL query can be run again by anyone and produce the same result, whereas a spreadsheet formula may reference hard-coded values or manual changes.
List scenarios where SQL is better than Excel (millions of rows, daily refresh, multiple users) and where Excel is sufficient (one-off analysis, small data).
Decide for a given analysis task (monthly revenue report vs. ad-hoc customer inquiry) whether SQL, Excel, or both should be used.

topics.title: INNER JOIN and LEFT JOIN
topics.description: Combine rows from two tables on a shared key using INNER JOIN (matched rows only) and LEFT JOIN (all left-table rows).

steps.d: Combine customers and orders using INNER JOIN on customers.id = orders.customer_id to match each order to its customer.

steps.t: Compare INNER and LEFT join results
steps.d: Write the same query using INNER JOIN and LEFT JOIN on a table with unmatched rows, then compare the row counts to see why LEFT JOIN returns more rows.
In a join, select from both tables — SELECT customers.name, orders.amount, orders.date — and use aliases if column names overlap.
Add WHERE to a join to show only orders after 2024-01-01 from customers in California.
Compare the joined result to the original tables to confirm the join is correct — no duplicates, no missed rows — by spot-checking a few values.

topics.title: RIGHT, FULL, and Multi-Table JOINs
topics.description: Complete the JOIN family with RIGHT and FULL OUTER JOINs, then chain multiple JOINs to pull data from three or more tables at once.

steps.t: Write a LEFT and RIGHT join
steps.d: Use LEFT JOIN to keep all left-table rows even if unmatched, or RIGHT JOIN to keep all right-table rows.
Use FULL OUTER JOIN to include all rows from both tables, with NULLs where there is no match.
Join three tables — customers to orders to order_details — using two JOIN clauses to pull customer name, order ID, and product name in one query.
Use table aliases (c for customers, o for orders) and qualify column names (c.id, o.customer_id) when the same column name appears in multiple tables.
Check that row counts make sense at each join step; if you join customers (100 rows) to orders (1000 rows) you should get roughly 1000 rows, not 100,000.

topics.title: Entity-Relationship Diagrams (ERDs)
topics.description: Read an ERD to identify primary and foreign keys, understand one-to-many relationships, and plan which tables to join before writing a single line of SQL.

steps.d: Study an ERD and identify primary keys (underlined), foreign keys (with arrows), and relationships (one-to-many, many-to-many) before writing any join.
Recognize when one customer has many orders, or one order has many line items, and plan your join accordingly.
For a multi-table query, decide which tables to join first based on the ERD, so you avoid accidental cross-products.
Use an ERD to find direct paths between tables (customers → orders → products) rather than guessing at join keys.

steps.t: Validate join keys match the ERD
steps.d: Verify that your join clauses match the foreign key relationships shown in the ERD, so you are joining on the correct columns.

topics.title: Partitioned Aggregations with OVER
topics.description: Use the OVER clause with PARTITION BY to compute SUM, COUNT, and AVG per group without collapsing rows the way GROUP BY does.

steps.t: Use OVER clause with PARTITION BY
steps.d: Write SELECT customer_id, amount, SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY region) to show total regional revenue alongside each order.
Show that GROUP BY collapses rows (one row per region) while OVER keeps all rows and adds an aggregate column.
Use PARTITION BY product_category, month to compute running sales totals per product per month without collapsing rows.
In one query, compute SUM and COUNT and AVG in separate OVER columns so you see multiple aggregates per partition.
Check that the aggregate value in each OVER column is the same for all rows in the same partition, confirming correctness.

topics.title: RANK, ROW_NUMBER, and DENSE_RANK
topics.description: Assign ordinal positions to rows within a partition — rank customers by spend, flag the top-N records per group, and understand the difference between RANK and DENSE_RANK.

steps.d: Assign row numbers 1, 2, 3 within each region using ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY region ORDER BY amount DESC).
Use RANK to assign 1, 2, 2, 4 when there are ties, or DENSE_RANK to assign 1, 2, 2, 3, and explain when each is appropriate.
Rank products by revenue within each region, then filter WHERE rank <= 3 to show the top 3 products per region.
Use NTILE to divide customers into quartiles by spend (quartile 1 = lowest 25%, quartile 4 = highest 25%).
Show the same data ranked with ROW_NUMBER, RANK, and DENSE_RANK side-by-side and explain the differences.

topics.title: LEAD, LAG, and Running Totals
topics.description: Compare a row to the previous or next row with LAG and LEAD, and build running totals and moving averages with ordered window frames.

steps.t: Compare a row to the previous row
steps.d: Use LAG(amount, 1) OVER (ORDER BY order_date) to see the prior order's amount next to the current order.
Use LAG to compute current_revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month) to see month-over-month dollar change.
Use LEAD(price, 1) OVER (ORDER BY date) to see what the next product's price is in the current row.
Use SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY order_date ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) to compute cumulative revenue.
Use AVG(amount) OVER (ORDER BY order_date ROWS BETWEEN 29 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) to compute a 30-day moving average of daily revenue.

topics.title: Common Table Expressions (CTEs) with WITH
topics.description: Define named result sets using WITH clauses so each logical step of a complex query can be read and tested independently.

steps.d: Write a CTE: WITH top_customers AS (SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) as total FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id) SELECT * FROM top_customers WHERE total > 10000.
Define one CTE for top customers, another for high-value orders, then join them in the main query to find customers with both traits.
Before using a CTE in a bigger query, run just the CTE part to verify it returns the right data and row count.
Use descriptive CTE names like top_10_regions, not t1 or temp, so reviewers can understand the logic without reading each line.
Add a comment above each CTE explaining what it computes, so someone maintaining the query later can understand your intent.

topics.title: Subqueries and Nested SELECT Statements
topics.description: Embed a SELECT inside another SELECT to filter on aggregated results, create derived tables, and solve problems that a single flat query cannot handle.

steps.d: Use SELECT customer_id FROM orders WHERE amount > (SELECT AVG(amount) FROM orders) to find orders above the average.
Create a subquery like SELECT * FROM (SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) as orders FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id) WHERE orders > 5.
Solve 'customers with above-average spend' by subquerying first for average, then filtering against that result.
Rewrite the same query using a subquery and using a WITH clause, and explain that both work but CTEs are often easier to read.
Run the subquery on its own to check the intermediate result, then verify the full query filters correctly against that result.

topics.title: Query Decomposition and Readability
topics.description: Refactor long one-liner queries into layered CTEs, add meaningful aliases, and apply formatting conventions that make SQL reviews fast.

steps.d: Take a 50-line query and split it into 3-4 named CTEs, each handling one logical step (filter, aggregate, rank, join).
Add AS total_revenue, not AS t, and use aliases in the main query so the output is self-documenting.
Put SELECT, FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY on separate lines, indent subqueries, and align join conditions so the structure is obvious.
Precede each CTE with a comment explaining its purpose, and add inline comments for non-obvious logic.

steps.t: Have a peer review your code
steps.d: Ask someone to read your query without asking you questions; if they struggle to understand it, simplify or add comments.

topics.title: Cohort Analysis and Funnel Queries
topics.description: Group users by acquisition week, track how they move through a funnel, and compute conversion rates at each step using window functions and CTEs.

steps.d: Assign each user a cohort_week based on their first purchase, then track how many users from each cohort returned in weeks 1, 2, 4, and 13.
Write a query that shows how many users completed each step (viewed product, added to cart, completed checkout, confirmed delivery) to identify where most abandon.
Use window functions to count users at each funnel step, then compute step_users / prior_step_users to get conversion % at each stage.
Show whether new users acquired in Jan have higher retention than those acquired in Feb by comparing the same metrics across cohort_month.
Verify that funnel row counts decrease at each step (or stay flat if there are edge cases), and validate the calculated conversion rates sum to a reasonable cohort return %.

topics.title: Churn and Retention Analysis
topics.description: Detect users who became inactive, compute monthly retention rates, and investigate the causes of an engagement drop with SQL case studies.

steps.d: Use a CTE to mark users who were active last month but inactive this month as churned; COUNT distinct churn cases to get a churn metric.
For each cohort_month, count how many of that month's new users remained active in month+1, month+2, etc. to build a retention curve.
Join the churn table to usage data to find patterns — did churned users have low engagement, or did they stop after a single purchase?
For churned users, calculate days_active (last_active_date - first_active_date) to see whether users churn fast or after months.
Compute churn % by month for the past 12 months and plot to see whether churn is rising, falling, or stable.

topics.title: Revenue Reporting and Business Metrics
topics.description: Write MRR and ARR roll-forward queries, segment revenue by product or region, and validate A/B test results directly in SQL.

steps.d: For each month, compute: (prior month MRR) + (new customer revenue) - (churned revenue) + (expansion revenue) - (downgrade revenue) = current MRR.
Break down revenue by product, region, customer segment, and sales channel in a single query to identify which segments are growing.
Count conversions in test and control groups, compute conversion rate and statistical significance directly in SQL.
Take monthly MRR and gross it up to ARR; break ARR into new, expansion, retention, and downgrade components.
Verify that your MRR roll-forward sums to total MRR, and that monthly figures match the accounting system before presenting results.

topics.title: Google BigQuery Free Tier Setup
topics.description: Activate BigQuery's sandbox, query Google's free public datasets, and understand the 1 TB/month free query allowance so you can practise at no cost.

steps.d: Visit console.cloud.google.com, activate the BigQuery API, and set up the sandbox — you'll get 1 TB of free queries per month and 10 GB of storage.

steps.t: Load a public dataset and run first query
steps.d: Open the bigquery-public-data project, choose 'bigquery-public-data:usa_names.usa_1910_current', and run: SELECT * FROM `bigquery-public-data.usa_names.usa_1910_current` LIMIT 10 to confirm access.
Click 'Estimate' in the BigQuery editor before running a query and note the 'Bytes billed' estimate; understand that scanning 1 GB costs approximately $0.005 in the free tier.

steps.t: Write three exploratory queries on public data
steps.d: Write and run: a count of rows per table, a filtered query (WHERE clause), and an aggregation (GROUP BY) on the public dataset to practice BigQuery syntax and become confident with it.
For the usa_names dataset, write down: row count, date range, columns available, and top 10 baby names by frequency — this confirms your queries are working and data is readable.

topics.title: Snowflake Trial and Cloud SQL Basics
topics.description: Set up a Snowflake 30-day trial, load sample data, and compare syntax differences between BigQuery standard SQL and Snowflake SQL.

steps.d: Register for a Snowflake account, pick a region, and load the sample TPC-H dataset provided in the trial environment.
Write a simple query (SELECT, WHERE, GROUP BY) in both BigQuery and Snowflake and note any syntax differences in keywords or functions.
Upload a CSV to Snowflake using the COPY command and verify the load succeeded by querying the table.
Create a Snowflake warehouse with S (small), M (medium), and L (large) compute, run the same query on each, and compare query time and credit cost.
Summarize the trade-offs between BigQuery (fully managed, pay-per-query) and Snowflake (warehouse sizing, COPY costs) for your use case.

topics.title: Query Cost Optimisation
topics.description: Read query execution plans, use columnar partitioning and clustering, avoid SELECT *, and estimate byte costs before running expensive scans.

steps.d: Run an EXPLAIN or EXPLAIN ANALYZE to see how the database will execute a query, and identify where the most time is spent.
Partition a table by date so queries filtering on date only scan relevant partitions, not the entire table.
Cluster a table by customer_id to group rows with the same ID together, speeding up JOIN and GROUP BY on that column.
Before running a query, estimate how many bytes it will scan (columns selected * rows queried) and multiply by your platform's cost per TB scanned.
Take an expensive query that uses SELECT *, has no partitioning, and scans 100 GB; rewrite it to select 5 columns, add date filtering, and reduce to 10 GB scanned.
